destructor:rack::audio::Port::~Port().finding: P1: none of the cited tests checks what happens when a port is destroyed. test_a_port_without_a_device keeps its port in KEPT until Rack quits; test_offsets_and_json drops `other` and asserts nothing afterwards; test_audio_in_live_rack only checks that the in-Rack suite passed. A broken ~PyAudioPort/release() (native/bindings/audio.cpp, PyAudioPort::~PyAudioPort and release) would pass all of them. Smallest fix: cite tests/laboratory/in_rack/test_audio_devices.py::test_audio_teardown_runs_no_python_and_leaves_ports_pointing_nowhere (it asserts `second.subscribed == []` after gc deletes the port) or tests/io/in_rack_virtual/test_virtual.py::test_active_stream_module_deletion_and_hotplug, or add an unsubscribe-on-delete assertion to test_audio.py.

field:rack::audio::Device::processMutex.finding: P1: the order in which RackPy takes processMutex and the GIL can deadlock. Rack's Device::processBuffer holds processMutex while it calls each port (Rack src/audio.cpp:37-49). PyAudioPort's overrides then take the GIL inside that lock on the Python-driven path (native/bindings/audio.cpp:134,151,163). Elsewhere RackPy takes processMutex while holding the GIL: subscriberList (audio.cpp:390), and Rack's Device::subscribe/unsubscribe (src/audio.cpp:22,27) reached from Port.set_device_id, Device.subscribe and port deletion with the GIL held. Two ways this hangs: (a) on one thread, a process_* override that reads self.device.subscribed or calls set_device_id locks the non-recursive processMutex its own thread already holds; (b) PythonDevice.process_buffer on a worker thread (the docs allow 'the calling Python thread') while the main thread reads .subscribed. Smallest fix: refuse processMutex-taking calls while the same thread is inside Device::processBuffer (a thread_local flag set in PythonDevice.process_buffer), and release the GIL before locking processMutex from Python-facing bindings.

field:rack::audio::Port::context.finding: P1: no test and no documentation. No test anywhere reads `port.context` for an audio port (searched tests/**). docs/reference/audio.md#audio-ports never mentions the `context` property or that it is read-only, although Rack's field is a writable public member (audio.hpp Port::context). Only the docstring at native/bindings/audio.cpp:886-889 explains it. Smallest fix: assert `port.context == raw.context_get()` in test_a_port_without_a_device, and add one line to the Ports doc section saying it is read-only and other contexts' ports are refused.

field:rack::audio::Port::driver.finding: P1: no cited test reads `port.driver`. test_a_port_without_a_device and test_offsets_and_json use get_driver(); the only `port.driver` read is in the uncited tests/laboratory/in_rack/test_audio_devices.py:192, where it is None. docs/reference/audio.md#audio-ports lists only 'The properties `driver_id`, `device_id` and `device`' and leaves out `driver`. Also, for a laboratory driver the property returns None while Rack's field is non-null (audio.cpp:884 looks the driver up by driverId, which is -1), and this is not documented. Smallest fix: assert `port.driver == port.get_driver()` in test_a_port_without_a_device, and document `driver` (and its None case for unlisted drivers) in the Ports section.

method:rack::audio::Device::onStartStrea.finding: P2: the record's fields don't match the code. It says gil_release=false, but PythonDevice.start_stream releases the GIL (native/bindings/audio.cpp:1045), as its own notes say. Its thread is 'main thread; live bound Rack UI context', but start_stream has no main-thread check (only DeviceLease), and docs/reference/audio.md#audio-python-drivers says it runs 'on the calling Python thread'. Smallest fix: set gil_release=true and give a thread value that matches the docs, or add requireMainThread.

method:rack::audio::Device::processBuffe.finding: P1: possible deadlock, and the record's fields are wrong. PythonDevice.process_buffer releases the GIL (audio.cpp:1073) and calls Rack's Device::processBuffer, which holds processMutex while calling ports (Rack src/audio.cpp:37-49). A Python port's override takes the GIL back inside that lock (audio.cpp:134,151,163). An override that calls self.device.subscribed (subscriberList, audio.cpp:390) or set_device_id (Device::unsubscribe/subscribe, src/audio.cpp:22,27) relocks the non-recursive processMutex on the same thread and hangs. Driving from a worker thread, which the docs allow, can also deadlock against a main-thread caller that holds the GIL and waits for processMutex. No test covers either case. The record also says gil_release=false, although the code releases it, and thread 'main thread', although there is no main-thread check. Smallest fix: refuse processMutex-taking bindings while the current thread is inside processBuffer (a thread_local flag), release the GIL before locking processMutex in bindings, and correct gil_release and thread.

method:rack::audio::Port::processBuffer(.finding: P0: out-of-bounds read and write. The input_offset/output_offset setters accept any int (native/bindings/audio.cpp:874,876). Rack passes `input + inputOffset` and `output + outputOffset` (Rack src/audio.cpp:45). For a negative offset, outputSpan computes `size_t(count)*stride - outputOffset` as count*stride + |offset| (audio.cpp:123). The Python-override path then copies with floatArray and writes back with copyBack (audio.cpp:139), touching |offset| floats before the start of the caller's buffer. That corrupts the heap whenever a port overriding process_buffer is driven by PythonDevice.process_buffer. Smallest fix: refuse negative offsets in the setters (Core Audio would also read out of bounds with them), or clamp the spans to the buffer and skip the copy when the offset is outside [0, count*stride); then add a regression test.

method:rack::audio::Port::processInput(c.finding: P0: out-of-bounds read. When input_offset is negative (the setter at native/bindings/audio.cpp:874 accepts it), Rack passes `input + inputOffset` (Rack src/audio.cpp:41). inputSpan (audio.cpp:122) wraps around to count*stride + |offset|. On the Python-override path, floatArray then reads |offset| floats before the caller's input buffer into the array given to process_input, so the override gets data from outside the buffer. Smallest fix: refuse negative offsets in the setter, or clamp inputSpan and skip the copy when the offset is out of range; then add a regression test.

method:rack::audio::Port::processOutput(.finding: P0: out-of-bounds write. When output_offset is negative (the setter at native/bindings/audio.cpp:876 accepts it), Rack passes `output + outputOffset` (Rack src/audio.cpp:49). outputSpan (audio.cpp:123) wraps around to count*stride + |offset|. copyBack (audio.cpp:167) then writes |offset| floats before the caller's output buffer on the Python-override path, which corrupts the heap. Smallest fix: refuse negative offsets in the setter, or clamp outputSpan and skip the copy when the offset is out of range; then add a regression test.
